newsitem.title: COLOMBIA: Government says Colombia coffee crisis not so bad.
newsitem.headline: Government says Colombia coffee crisis not so bad.

text.p: Colombia's Finance Minister Jose Antonio Ocampo stepped into the lion's den Thursday and told angry coffee growers that the crisis sweeping the sector was no worse than in the previous five years.

He conceded that international coffee prices had sunk to less than half the post-war average in 1996. But he played down the National Coffee Growers' Federation's predictions that the Coffee Fund could be saddled with a $465 million deficit by next September.

"I want to dispel...the impression that there is a confrontation between the government and coffee growers," Ocampo said. "Throughout the year, relations have been very cordial. Those who try to show the government as the coffee growers' enemy are wrong," he added.

Coffee growers, in the final day of a four-day congress, had hoped Ocampo would bring along a concrete package of prosposals and a budget allocation to combat the crisis, fueled by a strengthening peso, falling international prices and the devastating coffee-borer plague.

Instead Ocampo made vague promises of unspecified government financing to fund restructuring, adding that central bank targets for a more relaxed monetary policy and a devaluation of the peso in 1997 should offset some of the effects of the crisis.
The coffee growers threatened to convene a permanent congress until the government offers realistic solutions. No decision had been taken on this by early Thursday afternoon.
The current international price of Colombian coffee hovers between $1.10 and $1.30 per pound, which Ocampo said was less than half the average of real term prices since World War II.

In his address to the congress earlier this week, the head of the National Coffee Growers' Federation Jorge Cardenas warned that the crisis was so severe that the Coffee Fund -- jointly administered by the federation and the government -- may be unable buy Colombia's harvest in the 1997-1998 coffee year.

The fund has paid support prices to growers for their harvest for years. If it were no longer able to guarantee the purchase of all Colombian coffee it could open up the market to unbridled forces of supply and demand and leave growers to negotiate directly with private exporters.
But Ocampo predicted that the fund's deficit would not surpass 0.26 percent of Colombia's gross domestic product, which he said was in line with the 1995 deficit and only half that of 1991.

The finance minister reiterated the need for changes in the sector, including an increase in production, crop diversification and programs to retrain the workforce. He conceded a large proportion of coffee workers could lose their jobs as a result of the crisis but did not specify numbers.
